title: Build intelligent Android apps with Google's AI

segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
JOLANDA VERHOEF: Let's get started.
My name is Jolanda Verhoef, and I will be joined later
by my colleague Thomas.
Our approach to AI on Android is based on three core pillars.
So first of all, the Android operating system
is evolving into an intelligent system,
and you can expose your app's capabilities to that system.
Second, you can bring intelligence
into your app using Cloud and on-device models.
And finally, you can use developer productivity
to use intelligence to build your apps.
Now, together, these three pillars
represent our commitment to embedding intelligence
throughout the Android ecosystem.
And while all three of them are crucial to the future
of Android, today, I want to focus on this middle pillar.
So together with Thomas, we're going
to make sure that you learn everything
about in-app intelligence today.
Now, if you want to learn more about the other two pillars,
you can watch "What's new in Android"
to learn more about the first pillar, the intelligence system.
Or you can watch "What's new in Android development tools"
if you want to learn more about developer productivity.
Now, for today, we're going to, at a high level,
cover five different areas.
So I will start with on-device inference,
and then Thomas will be here to talk about cloud
and to talk about hybrid inference.
And I'll be back again to talk about agents
running in the cloud and how you can connect to them.
And then finally, we'll have a sneak preview
into running agents on device.
So how are we going to talk about those?
Well, what we want to do is we want
to take a travel app called Jetpacker,
which our team has been building over the past weeks/months.
And we're going to start with a very basic travel app.
And throughout the talk, we're going
to make that more personalized, intelligent, and agentic.
And so right now, the app already looks quite nice,
but it isn't yet using the newest intelligence APIs.
So I actually have the app running on my device.
So without further ado, let's have a look at it.
So let's have a look.
We should see my phone.
There we go.
And as you can see, we have the Jetpacker app running there.
So let's open it up.
And you can also see in the right top of my screen
that I'm actually currently in airplane mode,
so I don't have any internet connection.
And as you can see, I have my current California trip right
here.
We can look at our upcoming trips.
I'm going to Ireland later.
And then later this year, I'll be in Paris.
And we can have a quick look at our past trips as well.
So here, we have an overview of all our trips.
We can go to our Itinerary screen
to have a deeper look at what each of the days looks like.
And then we can also go to the Detail screen as well.
So far, so good.
Basic app, but it isn't yet using
any form of intelligent APIs.
So let's go back to our slides and have
a look at the first feature that we want to build.
So during today's session, we're going
to walk you through not one, not two,
but seven different intelligent features.
And so I think we should just get going with the first one.
So for our first feature, we're going
to look at our Itinerary screen.
We know from our users that that screen can actually
be quite overwhelming, especially when you
have a long trip coming up.
There's a lot of stuff happening.
So what we want to do, we want to create a card
at the top of the screen that summarizes the upcoming trip
and that includes some information
on how the user can best prepare for that trip.
So for this, what we'll do is we'll access a model
and we'll give it some input and we will get some outputs.
So in this case, we will give it the full trip itinerary.
And then as outputs, we will get a short summary
and we will get some tips on things to pack and phrases
to learn.
So this setup is actually a great candidate
for using an on-device model.
It has shorter inputs.
It has shorter outputs, making sure
that that on-device model can run really fast.
Now, when you use an on-device model, of course,
you have no additional cloud inference costs,
and we don't have to worry about internet connectivity,
since the model is going to be consistently working even when
we have spotty internet or if we have
no internet connection at all.
And given that we're traveling, that's
quite a nice feature to have.
So if we're going to want to build with on-device features,
we're going to have to use Gemini Nano.
Gemini Nano is Google's most efficient model
that is optimized for mobile devices.
We first introduced Nano a few years ago,
and by now, we have over 140 million devices
running versions of Nano.
And our latest version, Nano 4, is
based on the same architectural foundation as the recently
released Gemma 4 model, and then got further optimized
for maximum battery and performance efficiency.
Now, Gemini Nano 4 is coming to consumer devices
later this year, but as a developer,
you can already preview and prototype with it.
And so for today's demos, we're going
to use Gemini Nano 4 for our use cases
and show you how capable that model actually
is in a whole range of different scenarios.
So let's dive right into our code
using the ML Kit GenAI Prompt API.
This API gives us access to that Gemini Nano
model that runs on-device.
So with this API, we simply take our trip itinerary
and then we add it to our prompt,
and we ask our model to generate a summary of our trip,
along with tips on preparing for the trip.
Now, here, what I did is I just wrote a prompt myself.
I just sat down and thought, what would I ask this model?
And that's great, but we kind of want to iterate on that.
It's always good to test out a prompt
before you bring it to production and kind
of see how you can make it fit well with your use case.
So let's switch back to our phone and let's do just that.
So in order to do that, I'm going
to actually close my Jetpacker app for a second,

It is available on all devices that support AICore.
And if you don't have a physical device with that model

go to Android Studio and you can use the Gemma 4 model there.
So let's have a look at the AICore app.
As you can see, we have Gemini Nano 3 there,
but we also have Nano 4 Fast and we have Nano 4 Full.
So here, we can choose which of the models.
Now, I already downloaded them just

So let's start with the prompt that I

spending this much time generating this much text.
So this is where we start iterating.
Now, I did some of that iteration

be useful for us to look at.
So here, what I did is-- let's first take a look.
We got a very fast response.

1.6 seconds to generate it.

We immediately have it coming up.

Amazing.
Let's switch back to our slides.

And for me, if I'm traveling, one

So for such a tedious task, wouldn't it

this is another great use case for using an on-device solution

actually be processed locally on the device
without any of their data being sent to the cloud.
Nano 4 excels at multimodality, and so this especially
includes image understanding for tasks like OCR and visual data

So naturally, it will excel at extracting information
for our receipts as well.
So let's have a look at how this works.
In our last example, we only passed in a text prompt.

to be processed.

specify that we want three pieces of information here based
on the receipt.
We want a generated title.
We want to get an amount and a category.

we'll also tell the model that we
want it to return a certain JSON object.
So let's see this feature in action
before we continue with the slides.
Let's go to our phone, and let me quickly

I have to shake my phone in order to go to the debug menu.

Here we go.
Say hi, everyone.
Yay.
And let's take a picture.
There we go.

actually using the Gemini full model.
So you saw that we had a fast and we had a full model.
And in this case, we want to have that full image
recognition, so we're using that more complex model for us.
And as you can see, it recognizes
that we did an espresso blend purchase, which was $5.94.
That is correct.
Amazing.
Cool, let's go back to the slides.
[APPLAUSE]
I'm always so happy when demos actually work.
[LAUGHS] This one was the scariest one,
but hey, there we go.
And as you saw, this is already working pretty well, right?
But you might have noticed that we had to explain to the model
what kind of fields that we need,
and we had to give it a JSON example of what that then

And then after we wrote that whole prompt,
we then had to go and parse the return data, which

This is a lot of manual steps, and all of those manual steps
can go wrong.
So it's kind of scary.
And this is why we're introducing a Structured Output
API.
This API is going to land soon, but let
me give you a quick sneak preview
into what it will look like.
So with our Structured Output API,
we can mark any data class as generable.
And then we can further describe the class using guides
for each of the properties.
So these annotations basically guide the model
and tell it what kind of data it should generate.
If we do this, we can actually now, for our request,
simplify our prompt.
We don't have to guide it anymore there.
And then we can use the method called
generateTypedContentRequest that takes
the parsed receipt class name to restrict what
the expected output should be.
Let's make sure I don't lose my receipt.
And now, our response simply contains this parsed receipt
instance, or it will return null if it wasn't able to find one.
So with structured output, we can
be more confident about consistent outputs,
and our code is much, much simpler,
with Kotlin data classes that integrate seamlessly
with the Android code base.
Now, during this talk, we prototyped some pretty cool
features with on-device APIs using the latest Gemini Nano 4
preview model, but this is just the start.
We already have seen lots of apps using the Prompt
API in production to leverage the power of Gemini Nano for use
cases such as classification, summarization,
content inspiration, those kind of things.
If you want to learn more about how
you can get the latest in on-device Android,
you can check out this talk, where
we are going to go more in depth on how
you can ship on-device use cases to production.
Next, I will hand it off to Thomas,
who will walk you through the next couple of features.
[APPLAUSE]
THOMAS EZAN: Thank you, Jolanda.
So yeah, Gemini Nano 4 is pretty impressive,
and it's really exciting to see how on-device models are getting
better and better every year.
So we talked about Gemini Nano that is basically optimized
to run on your Android device efficiently,
but sometimes you have use cases that
require an AI model that has either a greater world
knowledge or a much larger context window,
or sometimes even greater ability in handling
complex tasks.
So let's take a look at what we can
build with these cloud models.
So we are going to use them to build our next feature
in the Jetpacker app.
So we are going to build a museum assistant.
So it will be a chatbot that is powered by Gemini Flash
and enables you to ask questions to plan your next visit to,
let's say, the Louvre Museum in Paris.
So first, you need to add the Firebase AI
Logic to your project.
And once you do that, with just a few lines of Kotlin code,
you can directly call the Gemini models
that are running in the cloud.
You will start by instantiating a generative model,
and you will pass the specific version of Gemini
that you want to use.
And then you basically just have to call start chat
to create a chat.
And the cool thing about the SDK is
that it will actually manage the chat history for you.
So the communication between your app and the model
is actually fully handled by the Firebase SDK.
There are three series of Gemini AI models
that are running in Google Cloud that you can use.
So there is Gemini Pro, which is really good for complex tasks.
There is Gemini Flash, which has a very low latency.
And Gemini Flash Lite, which offers
a really good intelligence cost ratio,
and also has a very low latency.
So we want to build a chatbot that is really
knowledgeable about the museum.
And earlier, I mentioned that cloud models
store massive amounts of world knowledge.
So you can assume that Gemini already
knows quite a lot about the Louvre,
but it doesn't necessarily know everything
there is to know about it.
So for example, if you ask the model
about the current temporary exhibitions
that are happening at the Louvre,
the chatbot will basically tell us to go to the website
and search for it ourselves.
So it's not super helpful.
So what we can do to prevent this is use
a technique called grounding.
So in the context window, which is the full input that
is passed to the model, we are going
to add some relevant content to help the model answer the user's
query better.
So grounding techniques are also used
in the context of Retrieval-Augmented Generation,
or RAG.
So you can implement it yourself,
but we also made it easy for you with the following APIs.
There is URL grounding, which enables
you to use a document at a specific URL,
there is maps grounding, which uses the data from Google Maps,
and there is web grounding that is using real-time web data.
So let's see how we can use them.
We are going to start with URL grounding.
So let's imagine that you want to prioritize
some data from a specific page that is hosted on the web.
So you will start by adding the URL context
tool to the list of tools when you instantiate the model.
And then in the user prompt, we will tell the model
to look at the specific page at the URL to grant the response.
And so you can see that here, we are actually using
the FAQ URL of the museum.
So here, we are only using one URL,
but you can actually use up to 20 URLs per request.
And so now, if we ask the chatbot about, for instance,
criteria to get discounted tickets, for example,
Gemini is going to actually use the content of the FAQ page
to answer.
So if I say, for example, if having a cat
named Mona Lisa grants you a discount
to get a ticket at the Louvre, you
will see that basically, the chatbot is saying no.
And as accurately outlined in the FAQ,
that is not enough to get a discount.
If we want to give the chatbot the ability
to retrieve some information from Google Maps,
we can use the Google Maps tool.
So that will, for instance, enable the chatbot
to search for cafes or restaurants
around the museum after our visit.
So if, after adding the tool, when I ask,
what are the best restaurants that
are good for children next to the Louvre,
we will actually get a pretty comprehensive response
from the chatbot.
It will query the data from Google Maps
and return a list of restaurants,
and it's actually anchoring on restaurants
that are clearly known for having a children's menu.
And so we can also use web search grounding
to, for instance, let the chatbot search for more
recent information on the web.
So we now have a pretty competent museum chatbot
to enable us to prepare the visit.
And so the cool thing is that we built all of that
with Gemini Flash in Firebase AI Logic.
And actually, the Gemini Pro and Gemini Flash models
are perfect to build, let's say, the first iteration of your AI
feature.
So whether you need multimodal understanding, JSON generation,
function calling, or even image generation,
you can quickly build everything in Kotlin
without really needing any server
code or any backend resources.
And the cool thing is that if your feature actually
doesn't rely on your own backend infrastructure,
you can really go to production with it and scale it.
You can use AI monitoring features
in the Firebase AI Logic SDK.
You can use server prompt templates
and App Check and basically scale to your whole user
audience.
And if you think about it, you probably already
have some features in your app that are good candidates
to use Gemini in Firebase AI Logic,
so I strongly encourage you to look into it.
So it's actually used already by hundreds of apps in production.
So for instance, the redBus application,
which is a ticketing platform, uses the Gemini
audio understanding capabilities to create
a voice-first, multilingual review system.
It's also used by Karrot, which is a marketplace app that
basically uses it to translate messages
between buyers and sellers.
Gratitude, a journaling app, is using
it to suggest journal entries.
And finally, UltraHuman, which is a fitness tracker app,
is using it to build a food logging feature using the Gemini
image understanding capabilities.
So a lot of interesting use cases.
OK, so let's take a step back for a second.
So we saw that many of you want to build
with Gemini Flash and Gemini Pro using cloud inference.
And earlier, Jolanda showed all the cool things
you can build with Gemini Nano on-device.
But we also heard some feedback from you.
You basically need to support users
on devices that don't necessarily
support Gemini Nano just yet.
So what if we could just combine both, right?
That's actually the promise of hybrid inference.
And I think I have a really good use case for it.
So reviews are a pretty key element in most Android
applications today.
So in your app, maybe you're asking your users
to write other users, or write a business, or even
a piece of content, like, I don't know, a song or a show.
And so you're often asking your users
to basically write a review, or sometimes you're
even asking users to post a review for your application
in Google Play.
And it's important for you, but it
can be sometimes tedious for your users.
So we think Gemini Nano can actually
be super helpful for that.
But you also need to have this feature
available on devices that don't support Gemini Nano just yet.
So in the Jetpacker app, earlier, the chatbot museum
recommended restaurants.
And so what if we were to implement a restaurant review
feature in the app?
So here, you can see that we have
a list of topics to choose from about how
we felt about the restaurant.
And we will let the model draft the short review for us.
And the user is always going to be able to edit it later
before posting it.
So here, you can see we are selecting some topics.
And once we are done, we are clicking
on generating the review.
And basically, if Gemini Nano is available on the device,
the review will be generated by Gemini Nano.
But if not, it will default to Gemini Flash Lite in the cloud.
So it's completely transparent for the users,
and it's also very easy for you to build as a developer.
So to build this, we are actually
using the latest API from Firebase AI Logic.

dependency to your project.
And then-- so you can see here that we basically
generate a review with a prompt that is interpolating
the selected topics.
And then when we instantiate the model,
you can see that we are passing an onDeviceConfig object, where
we define the inference mode that we want to use.
So here, you see that we are saying prefer on-device,
so we will prioritize on-device inference.
So this API supports four inference modes.
So there is prefer on device, prefer Cloud.
And there is also only on device and only cloud.
And it's actually available today, so you can try it out
and you can learn more about it in the Firebase documentation.
So we just talked about a very simple routing logic.
Here, it's basically two criteria.
Is Gemini Nano available on the device?
And is the device online?
But sometimes you want to build something
that is a little bit more complex,
so you can imagine having a pretty advanced custom routing
logic.
So for instance, you can monitor the system health of the device,
and you can decide to use a cloud
model if, let's say, the CPU is overloaded

And another thing worth checking is also the latency.
So if the latency is above a specific threshold,
you can decide to focus on on-device.
Another thing, too, to keep in mind,
is that not every single query requires
a very advanced model running in the cloud, and some do.
So it can be interesting sometimes
to use a lightweight LLM, like for instance, the Gemma 3
model that is only 270 million parameters,
to basically route those queries based on their complexity.
And at the end of the day, I'm just listing three criterias
here, but there are many other criteria
that you want to take into account based on your app's
needs or also the user experience that you
want to provide.
So if we go back to the Jetpacker app,

staff and the customers.
So the customers and the hotel staff

We also want low latency.

But there are already experiments
